Service Desk

User manual

How to ask for help, and how the desk answers. For everyone in the company who sends a request, and for the agents, leads and managers who work the queues.

Applies to Six7 Service Desk 0.1.0 (alpha). Screens show the demo company.

1. Getting started#

1.1 What the Service Desk is for#

When you need something from IT, HR or Facilities, you email them or fill in a short form, as you're used to. The Service Desk turns each request into a ticket: it gets a number, an owner and a time by which it will be answered, and you get an email that says so. Replies come back by email, in the same thread.

For the people on the desk, it's where the queues live: every ticket already has an owner when it arrives, the targets are measured, and nothing waits in a shared inbox.

Why Six7, and how its apps work, is in the Suite manual.

1.2 Opening the app#

Open the link you were given and bookmark it. Google signs you in with your work account: there's no separate password. See Suite §5 if you use several Google accounts.

You don't need the app to ask for help: email works on its own. The app shows your requests in one place.

1.3 Your role#

  • Everyone in the company can ask for help. The app shows you My requests and New request.
  • Agents answer the tickets of their queues. Queue Leads also run a queue. Managers look after a whole audience: the company's own requests (Internal), customers' (External), or both. Admins run the desk.

Your role shows at the top right when you're on the desk. How roles work in every Six7 app is in Suite §6. People outside the company never use the app: customers write and receive email, or use the contact form.

2. A tour of the app#

2.1 My requests#

Your requests, and the ones you're copied on, with their status and when they were last updated. Click one to read the conversation and act on it (§3.2). New request asks for something new.

2.2 My queue, the desk's home screen#

The bar at the top has My queue, Tickets, Board, Resources and Reports, and Admin tools for those who use it. On the right: Search tickets, New ticket, Away, a refresh button, and your initials, which open Your settings (the theme).

My queue shows what needs you, with a count for each list:

  • Breached: past a target;
  • Due soon: 75% of the target used;
  • Replies waiting: requesters answered;
  • To dispatch: new tickets held for you to assign, if you dispatch a queue;
  • Unassigned: nobody was free to take them; the leads know;
  • Mine: your open tickets, by next due time.

Each row shows the number, title, requester, queue, priority, status and time left ("2 h 10 m left", "45 m overdue"). Queue Leads, Managers and Admins also see By agent and Away agents, and a line that says whether email intake is running. At the top right, switch between Mine and your queues (Managers: their audiences).

2.3 A ticket#

The conversation on the left: the requester's emails, the replies, the acknowledgement the desk sent, internal notes on a tinted background, and single lines for what happened ("Assigned to Andrés Molina by rule: fewest open (2)"). The box to answer is below it.

On the right: the status, the owner and why they got it, the audience and queue, priority, category, service level and confidential flag; the two clocks (first response and resolution) with their due times; the requester and their other open tickets; Links and Similar; and the actions.

2.4 Tickets#

Every ticket your queues can see, newest first, with filters for everything: audience, queue, status, priority, service level, assignee (Me, Unassigned or a person), how it was assigned, SLA state (breached, due soon, on time), category, organisation, channel, confidential, and dates. Save filter keeps a set of filters in your browser. Export to Sheets exports the list as filtered (§5).

2.5 Board#

A queue's tickets as columns: New, Open, Waiting on requester, Waiting on others and Resolved (until they close). Each card shows the number, priority, title, owner and time left, with Due soon or Breached when it applies. Move to… changes the status, by the same rules as the ticket.

2.6 Resources#

The canned replies, links and short answers your queues keep, grouped by queue and category, with Open and Copy link. Queue Leads also Add, Edit and Deactivate them (§3.11).

2.7 Reports#

Five reports about the desk: chapter 6.

3. Everyday tasks#

3.1 Ask for help#

By email, as always: write to the queue's address (for example it@, hr@ or facilities@). You get an acknowledgement with the ticket's number and the time by which you'll get an answer.

In the app:

  1. Click New request.
  2. Choose the Queue and the Category. Under some categories, Before you wait shows help that may answer your question at once.
  3. Write a Subject and a Description: what happened, what you expected, and anything you tried.
  4. Tick This stops me from working if it does: it raises the priority to High.
  5. Copy colleagues if they should follow it (Colleagues to copy), and add files if you need to: up to 5, 10 MB each and 20 MB in all.
  6. Click Send request.

Customers email the company's help address, or use the contact form on its website. They never need the app.

3.2 Follow your request#

Replies come by email, and also show in My requests. Open a request to:

  • reply or Add file, then Send. Replying to the desk's emails works the same way;
  • Cancel request…, with a reason, if you no longer need it;
  • when it's Resolved: It's solved closes it, and Reopen… sends it back, with what still isn't right;
  • once it's Resolved or Closed, rate it under How did we do?: Good or Not good, with an optional comment, then Send rating. Only the person who asked can rate, once. A Not good with a comment reopens a Resolved request;
  • when it's Closed: write in the box and click Send as a new request. It opens a new request that names this one.

The resolution email asks "Did this solve it? Yes / No": answer there if you prefer. A request closes on its own 5 days after it's resolved, unless you reply.

3.3 Work your queue#

Start from My queue, top to bottom: Breached, then Due soon, then Replies waiting, then Mine by next due time.

  • New tickets arrive already assigned: most queues give each ticket to the first available agent at once.
  • Take gives you a ticket from To dispatch or Unassigned.
  • The ticket says who it's waiting for while it has no owner.

3.4 Reply, or write an internal note#

In the box under the conversation:

  • Reply (the default) goes to the requester by email, in their own thread, from the queue's address. Send, Send and wait on requester or Send and resolve.
  • Internal note is only for the desk: nothing is emailed. Add note.
  • Insert… adds a canned reply or a link from Resources, with the requester's name filled in. Those of the ticket's queue and category come first.
  • Cc copies people on the reply. Files can't be added to a reply in this release: ask for them by email, or add them on a New ticket.

Your first public reply stops the first-response clock. Replying to an unassigned ticket of your queue makes it yours.

3.5 Change a ticket's status#

ActionWhenWhat happens
Waiting on requester…You need something from themThey're emailed what you asked; the clock pauses until they reply
Waiting on othersYou wait for a supplier, another queue or a linked ticketThe ticket stays yours; Resume when it moves again
Resolve…It's doneA reply or a resolution note is required. The requester gets it with "Did this solve it? Yes / No"
Cancel ticket…It shouldn't be workedA reason is required, and the requester gets it by email

A requester's reply reopens a resolved ticket, and a reply to a closed one opens a new ticket that names it.

3.6 Correct priority, category, service level or privacy#

In the ticket's panel, change Priority, Category or Service level, then Save changes. The due times are recomputed. Tick or untick Confidential to say who may see the ticket (§4).

If someone else changed the same field while you were editing, the ticket says Someone else changed this: choose Keep mine or Use theirs.

3.7 Assign, release or transfer#

  • Assign… (Queue Leads, Managers and Admins): to anyone active in the ticket's queue.
  • Release… (the owner, a Queue Lead, a Manager or an Admin): hand it back with a reason. The rule gives it to someone else available.
  • Transfer…: to any queue, of either audience. The ticket keeps its requester, clocks and conversation, and gets an owner in the new queue. Replies then go out from the new queue's address, in the same thread.

A confidential ticket shows its whole conversation to the new queue. The dialog says so and offers Hand over as a linked ticket: a new ticket in the other queue with only what you write, linked to this one.

3.8 Open a ticket for someone#

For a request that came by phone or in person: New ticket at the top.

  1. The Requester's email: a colleague's or a customer's. An outside requester goes to a customer queue.
  2. The Queue and Category, the Subject and the Description (their words, which become the first message).
  3. The Priority, if not the category's default.
  4. Confidential, people to Copy, and files, if needed.
  5. Create ticket. It's routed, assigned and acknowledged like an email.

3.9 Link tickets, and handle an outage#

In the ticket's Links:

  • Link… joins two tickets you can see, by number, across queues. Each shows the other, and when one is resolved the other's owner hears.
  • New linked ticket… opens a ticket in any queue, linked both ways, for work another team must do.
  • For an outage, when many people report the same thing: Make parent on one ticket, then Link as duplicate… on the others (or Add duplicates… from the parent). On the parent, Reply to all answers every requester in their own thread, and Resolve parent and duplicates… resolves them all at once.

3.10 Go Away#

Click Away at the top, with a Back at time if you know it, then Switch Away. New tickets stop coming to you, and at the next run your tickets without a first reply go to someone available. Tickets you've started stay with you, and your lead sees them. Click again when you're back.

3.11 Use Resources and Similar#

  • Resources holds your queues' canned replies, links and short answers. Insert… in the reply box adds one to an answer.
  • Similar, on a ticket, lists up to five resolved tickets of the queue with words of the title in common, and how they were solved. Use in reply starts your answer from one.
  • Queue Leads keep Resources: Add, Edit and Deactivate. A link or snippet marked Public also helps requesters before they wait (§3.1).

4. Working with others#

How a request moves through the desk, and who acts at each step. Your company may work differently today: compare it with these pages before the desk goes live. The Configuration manual's §1.5 says what your Admin can change and what this release fixes.

4.1 A request's journey#

From the request to closing, the desk does most of the steps by itself; a person acts at the start and in the work itself.

4.2 Ticket statuses#

A ticket is always in one of seven statuses. §3.5 says what each action does.

4.3 Who gets a new ticket#

Inside the queue's hours, every ticket has someone accountable from its first minute: its owner, or the people who will give it one. Each queue chooses how: with Auto, the default, the rule picks at once; with Hold, a dispatcher has the first 15 minutes (by default); with Manual, a lead always decides. The ticket shows how it got its owner, for example "assigned by rule: fewest open (2)".

4.4 When a target is at risk#

Every ticket has two targets: its first reply and its resolution. As each target's clock runs, the desk acts by itself at three points, once per clock. A change of priority or service level recomputes the targets, so a step can come again.

4.6 Working together#

  • Confidential tickets are seen only by the members of their queue, the Managers of that queue and Admins. Files on internal notes, on any ticket, open only for those same people.
  • Copied colleagues get the replies and see the request in their My requests.
  • Chat. Your queue may post to its Google Chat space: new tickets to dispatch or that nobody can take, due soon, breached, overdue, and intake stopping.
  • Two people, one ticket. If someone else saved the same field while you were editing, choose Keep mine or Use theirs (§3.6).

5. Finding things#

  • Search tickets, at the top: a ticket's number, words of its subject, a requester or an organisation. It finds only what you may see.
  • Tickets has every filter (§2.4). Save filter keeps a set in your browser.
  • Export to Sheets on Tickets exports the whole filtered list, every page, as a Google Sheet. It opens on Google's Make a copy page, which saves it in your own Drive.
  • Copy link on a ticket copies its address, for a colleague who can see it.

6. Reports#

Reports shows five reports over the tickets you can see, each with a chart, a table and a sentence that sums it up. Choose the Weeks back, Audience, Queue, Priority, Level, Category and Organisation at the top.

ReportAnswers
VolumeHow many tickets came in each week, by which channel, and how many were resolved?
Service level performanceHow often did we meet the first-response and resolution targets, per queue, priority and customer?
Backlog and agingWhat's open now, how old, and how much is unassigned, held, waiting or breached?
Agent workload and speedEach person's open and resolved tickets, their response and resolution times, and satisfaction
Top categories and organisationsWhich categories and which customers raise the most tickets

Each report has Export to Sheets, Generate report (Doc) and Download PDF; Generate full report and Download full PDF make one document with all five. Copy link shares the report with its filters. The scope line says what's counted: your queues, an audience, or the whole desk.

7. For leads and managers#

Queue Leads:

  • To dispatch (in queues that hold), Unassigned, By agent and Away agents in My queue;
  • Assign… to anyone in the queue, ignoring Away and the limit of open tickets, and reopen cancelled tickets;
  • the breach emails, one per run, and Chat;
  • Admin tools › Intake: emails that need a person, such as an outsider writing to an internal address. Create ticket in a customer queue, Retry or Ignore;
  • Admin tools › Test routing: where an email would go, before it arrives;
  • the queue's Resources;
  • the desk overview email, daily or weekly, if your Admin set it.

Managers:

  • My queue and the Board for their audiences' queues;
  • working the tickets they see, as agents do: reply, note, change status, transfer and release; assigning, and reopening cancelled tickets;
  • Admin tools › Intake and Test routing, as leads have;
  • the overdue emails (the third rung of escalation);
  • reports across queues, and the desk overview for their audiences;
  • Validate data, after the desk's setup changes.

8. Email and notifications#

If you ask for help, you get the acknowledgement, the desk's replies, a "waiting on you" email when they need something, and the resolution with "Did this solve it?". All come from the queue's address, in your thread.

If you're on the desk, you're told by email when a ticket is assigned to you, a requester replies, a ticket is due soon, a linked ticket is resolved or a rating comes in: at once, or in your daily digest, as your Admin set it. The daily digest arrives around 07:00 on days there's something: your breached, overdue and due-today tickets, replies waiting, and for leads, their queue's breaches, unassigned and held tickets, away agents and the Intake log's waiting items.

Your settings (your initials, top right) holds your Theme: System, Light or Dark, kept on this device.

9. Using it with Gmail and Gemini#

  • Requesters never leave their email. Every reply is an email in their own thread, and their answers join the ticket.
  • View original email, on a message that came by email, shows the whole email as it arrived.
  • The Service Desk Gem, if your Admin has set it up, answers from your team's documents in the Gemini side panel. Resources links to it.

10. Using it on a phone#

The Service Desk works in your phone's browser; there's no app to install.

  • My requests and New request fit the screen.
  • On a ticket, the conversation comes first, then the panel with the fields, clocks and actions.
  • On the Board, Move to… changes a status (the board has no dragging, on any device).
  • Open links from the desk's emails in your browser, not inside the Gmail app.

11. When something goes wrong#

What you seeWhat it means
No acknowledgement after emailing a queueIt can take up to 5 minutes, and you get at most one an hour. Check your spam; if it's still not there, ask the queue's lead
"Someone else changed this"Another person saved the same field. Choose Keep mine or Use theirs
"Google is busy right now. Please try again in a moment." or "The app is busy"Many changes at once. Try again
"You can't see this ticket"It's in a queue you're not in, or it's confidential
"Email intake stopped" (leads)The desk isn't reading email. Tell your Admin at once
A ticket went to the wrong queueTransfer… it, and tell your lead so the rule can be fixed
"You don't have access to Six7 Service Desk yet"Email the queue's address instead, or ask an Admin to add you
"Six7 Service Desk is parked"The desk is stopped for now. Email and form requests wait, and become tickets when it's back. Ask the desk's Admin when that will be

Who to ask: your queue's lead, then the desk's Admin.

A. Appendix: keyboard#

Everything works from the keyboard: Tab moves between controls, Enter opens or presses them, and Esc closes a dialog or clears the search.

B. Appendix: words used in the app#

WordMeaning
TicketOne request, with a number such as TKT-0042
RequestA ticket, as the person who asked sees it
RequesterThe person who asked
QueueA team that answers, such as IT, HR or Help
AudienceWho asks: Internal (the company's people) or External (customers and outsiders)
Agent, Queue Lead, Manager, AdminThe desk's roles
Owner / AssigneeThe person working on a ticket
DispatcherSomeone who assigns a queue's new tickets during a hold
HoldA short wait for a queue's dispatchers before the rule assigns a new ticket
Service levelThe targets for a first response and for resolution, by priority
First responseThe first public reply by a person
Due soon, Breached, Overdue75% of a target used, the target passed, and 150% of it
Waiting on requesterThe desk needs something from them; the clock pauses
Waiting on othersThe desk waits for someone else; the ticket stays open
Resolved, ClosedDone; closed 5 days later, unless the requester replies
ConfidentialSeen only by the queue, its Managers and Admins
Internal noteA message only the desk sees
Parent, DuplicateAn outage's main ticket, and the tickets that report the same thing
IntakeThe desk reading email and forms, every 5 minutes
